title: Laser powder bed fusion of modified high entropy alloys
abstract: Abstract This review compiles and analyzes the current state of the art of modified high entropy alloys (MHEAs) processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), establishing composition-processing-microstructure-property relationships that define their printability, structural integrity, and performance. After contextualizing HEA/MHEA concepts and LPBF‑specific solidification phenomena, the review places particular emphasis on the modification strategies that tailor phase stability, melt‑pool behavior, and processability. These include targeted alloying additions, principal‑element ratio adjustments, and microalloying routes to stabilize FCC/BCC/B2 phase composition, mitigate cracking, and enable precipitation strengthening or microstructural refinement under LPBF’s rapid thermal cycles. A second major focus is the correlation between these compositional modifications and the resulting mechanical properties in both the as‑built and post‑processed conditions. The compiled data reveals distinct strength-ductility regimes across Cantor‑type alloys, Al‑containing dual‑phase systems, and refractory BCC‑based MHEAs, demonstrating how specific elemental additions, phase engineering strategies, and post‑processing treatments modulate hardness, tensile behavior, elongation, and failure modes. The comparative analysis highlights the strong dependency of mechanical properties on controlled phase fractions, segregation behavior, precipitates distribution, and defects. Overall, this review shows that the successful deployment of LPBF‑processed MHEAs critically depends on composition‑aware process design, where alloy modification strategies and mechanical property requirements must be jointly optimized.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High entropy alloys (HEAs) have garnered significant attention due to their unique compositional design and exceptional property profiles. Unlike conventional alloys, which are typically based on one principal element, HEAs consist of multiple elements mixed in high concentrations. This unconventional design strategy leads to the emergence of core effects such as high configurational entropy, sluggish diffusion, matrix distortion, and the cocktail effect, all of which contribute to the formation of simple solid-solution phases and can result in remarkable mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties [ 1 ,  2 ]. These materials can exhibit an excellent combination of high strength and ductility, superior thermal stability, corrosion and oxidation resistance, and promising behavior at both cryogenic and elevated temperatures [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Before HEAs, metallic alloys were generally composed of one or two main elements, to which small amounts of other elements were added. An illustrative example is iron-based alloys, where the incorporation of certain elements allows for the optimization of their properties.

The outstanding properties of HEAs make them strong candidates for use in demanding engineering applications across the aerospace, automotive, energy, and biomedical sectors [ 8 ]. For instance, their thermal stability and wear resistance are advantageous for turbine components and cutting tools, while their corrosion resistance is appealing for marine and chemical environments. Despite these advantages, challenges such as compositional control, processability, and cost-effective manufacturing have limited their widespread adoption. In this context, Additive Manufacturing (AM) is increasingly being explored to unlock the full potential of HEAs and overcome traditional processing limitations [ 9 ].

sections.heading: Core effects
paragraphs: The high configuration entropy present in the matrix brings unique effects that have impact on the properties of the HEAs. These effects resulting from the alloy composition are one of the main aspects that make high entropy alloys so promising. There are four main effects briefly addressed in this section, each with their individual causes and implications [ 2 ,  13 ].

sections.heading: High entropy effect
Slow diffusion
paragraphs: Slow diffusion in HEAs stems from their multi-principal-element complexity and high configurational entropy, which create heterogeneous local environments unlike conventional alloys [ 2 ,  15 ]. This heterogeneity broadens the distribution of energy barriers for atom jumps, hindering mobility. Two mechanisms dominate: (1) Fluctuations in bonding energy, due to disparities in atomic size, charge, and interactions, produce a rugged energy landscape that slows atomic “jumping” [ 15 ]. (2) Vacancy trapping occurs when defects fall into low-energy neighborhoods, reducing their mobility and thus overall diffusion [ 16 ]. Together, these mechanisms suppress atomic transport and contribute to the stability of HEAs, while making heat treatments more challenging because sluggish diffusion delays homogenization and stress relief. A comparison between a pure metal and a HEA is shown in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Diagram of atomic diffusion in pure metal alloys and high entropy alloys with hypothetical potential energies for each atomic position

sections.heading: Lattice distortion
paragraphs: In HEAs, multi-principal compositions produce a chemically heterogeneous matrix where severe lattice distortion arises from three sources, as shown in Fig.  2 : (1) atomic radius mismatch; (2) variations in electronegativity/bond energy that perturb local interactions; and (3) configurational disorder from random site occupancy [ 17 ,  18 – 19 ]. This distortion has mixed implications: it can strengthen the material via solid-solution hardening and raise yield strength, while enhancing high-temperature stability by suppressing diffusion. Conversely, it often lowers electrical and thermal conductivity, can reduce ductility and promote brittle fracture (notably at low temperatures or with large size mismatch) [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Overall, lattice distortion is a tunable but double-edged design lever that must be balanced to the target application. Fig. 2 Diagram representing the crystalline lattice of  a  a conventional alloy, and  b  a high entropy alloy

sections.heading: Cocktail effect
paragraphs: The cocktail effect in HEAs is based on the interaction between the multiple constituent elements, resulting in properties different from those expected from a simple rule of mixtures, almost resembling an atomic composite. This phenomenon occurs due to the complexity and heterogeneity of the matrix, leading to distortion in the crystal lattice, and is further amplified by the high mixing entropy, which stabilizes solid solution phases. All this affects atomic interactions in potentially unforeseen ways [ 1 ]. This cocktail effect can result in positive or negative changes in the mechanical properties of the alloy [ 24 ]. These attributes make the cocktail effect a key focus for the study and development of HEAs due to its significant impact on the mechanical properties of these materials.

sections.heading: Types of high entropy alloys
paragraphs: The design flexibility of High Entropy Alloys has given rise to several families, each tailored to meet specific structural or functional requirements, and with exceptional physical, chemical and mechanical properties. The following types of HEAs can be considered: Low-density HEAs (LDHEAs)—often incorporating lightweight elements such as Al, Mg or Ti, aiming to have a low density without sacrificing mechanical properties. These alloys are especially attractive for aerospace and automotive applications, where weight reduction is critical to improving fuel efficiency and performance [ 25 ,  26 – 27 ]. Refractory HEAs (RHEAs)—composed primarily of refractory metals with high melting points, such as W, Ta, Mo, Nb, Hf and Zr [ 28 ]. These alloys are engineered to operate under extreme thermal and mechanical loads, making them suitable for high-temperature applications [ 5 ]. High Entropy Shape Memory Alloys (HESMAs)—represent a unique subset that exhibits reversible deformation behaviors under thermal or mechanical stimuli, combining shape memory effects and superelasticity with high mechanical strength and thermal stability [ 7 ]. Modified HEAs (MHEAs)—refer to compositions that modify a base alloy with the intention to enhance its physical, chemical or mechanical properties, and sometimes even attaining functional properties, often through the addition of new elements [ 29 ].
These diverse HEA families demonstrate the vast potential of high entropy design principles in addressing the next generation of engineering challenges across multiple industries.

sections.heading: Low-density high entropy alloys
paragraphs: LDHEAs stand out due to their low density, usually less than 6 g/cm 3 , coupled with good mechanical properties. The mechanical properties/density ratio is essential for aerospace and automotive vehicles, not only for energy efficiency but also for reducing operational costs and ensuring safety, factors that are, for example, particularly important in the aviation sector, where safety is the top priority and operational cost reduction can lead to savings for airline customers. Typically, LDHEAs contain lightweight elements, such as Al, Ti, Mg, Be, and Si. Representative examples include the alloy AlNbTiV, with an approximate density of 5.2 g/cm 3  [ 30 ], and the more complex composition Al 20 Be 20 Fe 10 Si 15 Ti 35  (at.%), which combines lightweight elements with iron (Fe) to optimize mechanical properties [ 6 ]. Alloys such as AlNbTiV exhibit a compressive yield strength of about 1100 MPa at 600 °C and a compressive strain of approximately 12%, demonstrating the versatility of these alloys [ 31 ]. While the original HEA concept aimed to suppress intermetallics, the balance between low density and mechanical properties in LDHEAs is often achieved by engineering a microstructure that combines ductile solid solution phases with controlled intermetallic precipitates for strengthening. This tailored multi-phase approach provides a specific strength superior to conventional alloys.

sections.heading: Refractory high entropy alloys
paragraphs: RHEAs are a category of HEAs designed for high-temperature environments. These alloys leverage the high-entropy effect to stabilize structures, usually BCC, making them ideal for applications that require exceptional thermal resistance [ 32 ]. Notable examples include TiZrNbHfTa, with plastic deformation greater than 50% at room temperature, and compositions like WNbMoTa and (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5  (at.%), with the latter reaching yield strengths of 1000 MPa at 800 °C [ 35 ]. These alloys not only exhibit good mechanical properties at high temperatures, but also generally show good resistance to corrosion, making them excellent candidates for applications in the nuclear sector [ 32 ]. This type of alloy is recognized for its potential to replace nickel-based superalloys, offering a promising alternative for sectors operating under high temperatures and aggressive environments [ 33 ], but in applications where low density will not be a critical factor.

sections.heading: Shape memory high entropy alloys
paragraphs: In the last decade, the concept of HEAs has expanded the design for functional materials, in particular for shape memory alloys (SMAs). SMAs operate through a martensitic phase transformation, exhibiting shape memory effect or superelasticity [ 34 ]. HESMAs can exhibit a wide range of transformation temperatures, high recoverable strain, and better stability to temperature cycles [ 7 ]. In HESMAs, the selection of alloying elements is guided by both thermodynamic criteria and functional requirements. Recent studies have shown that small variations in chemical composition can be used to adjust transformation temperatures and optimize the balance between strength and ductility [ 7 ]. The microstructure of HESMAs typically consists of a matrix phase with high symmetry, such as a B2 phase (a BCC ordered phase) that transforms into a low-symmetry martensitic phase during cooling or under applied stress [ 35 ]. The complex matrix, resulting from the relatively large quantities of different elements in the HEAs, leads to a high density of precipitates, which can act both as nucleation sites and as barriers to the movement of linear defects in the matrix [ 36 ]. For example, studies with (TiZrHf) 50 Ni 25 Co 10 Cu 15  (at.%) alloys have shown significant improvement in recoverable strain and creep resistance compared to conventional NiTi alloys [ 37 ]. In another example, the development of (TiHfZr) 74 (NbTa) 26  (at.%) alloys, showed that controlled heat treatments can lead to a microstructure that favors full and stable superelastic recovery at high temperatures [ 38 ].

The exceptional physical, mechanical and functional properties of HESMAs make them ideal candidates for applications in the aerospace, automotive, and biomedical sectors. Their high-temperature stability and fatigue resistance allow their use in environments where conventional SMAs cannot be used. The ability to adjust phase transformations by changing alloy composition opens numerous possibilities for multifunctional applications, such as actuators, sensors, and energy conversion devices [ 20 ]. Future research focused on compositional modification, microstructural control, and advanced computational modeling should further refine HESMAs, paving the way for applications in high-performance and high-temperature environments.

sections.heading: Modified high entropy alloys
paragraphs: MHEAs represent a strategic evolution from the initial concept of equiatomic, single-phase HEA, whose primary motivation is to engineer the alloy to achieve a desired set of properties. This category includes HEAs whose compositions are intentionally adjusted to optimize specific properties of a base alloy, thereby overcoming its intrinsic limitations and expanding its versatility [ 29 ]. The modification strategies, which include adjusting the ratios of the principal elements, introducing targeted minor alloying additions, or substituting elements, allow for the tuning of microstructural features and, consequently, of mechanical and functional characteristics such as strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature stability [ 39 ]. By shifting principal elements ratios, designers can tune phase stability and fraction to manipulate the balance between different phases (e.g. FCC, BCC, B2, HCP), thereby navigating classic tradeoffs between strength, ductility, and toughness [ 40 ]. For instance, promoting FCC + BCC duplex microstructures can raise strength while preserving reasonable plasticity, whereas full BCC/B2 microstructures favor high hardness and creep resistance for elevated temperature service. Small additions (typically < 5 (at.%)) provide further levers: C, N, and B drive carbide, nitride and boride precipitation, respectively, and solution strengthening; Al and Si can enhance oxidation resistance via protective scale formation; Cr and Mo support corrosion resistance; and Nb/Ti containing precipitates enable precipitation hardening or, when controlled, dispersion strengthening. These compositional adjustments also refine grain size, and tailor thermal stability and magnetic or electrical responses, thereby translating promising baseline HEAs into alloys that meet specific design envelopes for wear, fatigue, and high temperature performance.

As an example, the base alloy CrFeCoNi, a four-element HEA with an FCC structure, is modified by the addition of aluminum to form Al X CrFeCoNi [ 41 ]. This addition influences phase formation and mechanical properties, particularly under high-speed deformation conditions. This system has been studied for its remarkable resistance to shear stress failure, which is crucial for applications in structural components subject to dynamic loads [ 42 ]. The content of aluminum is varied enabling a systematic study of how Al influences the alloy's structure, transitioning from FCC to BCC or mixed phases, which affects the mechanical properties [ 41 ,  43 ]. With the Al X CrFeCoNi system it is possible to increase the strength to weight ratio and the corrosion resistance, depending on the required application, as demonstrated by Arun et al. [ 44 ]. Another example is the base alloy AlCrTiV, an equiatomic HEA with high hardness and low density. To further increase its hardness, it is possible to alloy it with other elements in small atomic percentages, thereby modifying and enhancing its base properties. These modifications can involve adding small amounts of carbon, silicon, or boron, ranging from 0 to 5 (at.%), forming secondary phases. With the addition of 5 (at.%) B, the most significant increase was observed, with hardness rising to 710 HV [ 45 ]. More recently Abrantes et al. [ 29 ] showed that it is possible to modify Ti–6Al–4V as a base alloy and add nickel and cobalt to improve mechanical properties and achieve functional property, in this case, shape memory effect.

The modification strategies are numerous, demonstrating that MHEAs are a promising approach to alloy design. In practice, MHEAs bridge discovery and deployment by coupling chemical composition and microstructure control with processability and reliability requirements, enabling qualification pathways for a plethora of applications.

sections.heading: Objectives
paragraphs: The primary objective of this review is to provide a comprehensive and critical survey of the current state of the art of modified high entropy alloys fabricated via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). This work aims to synthesize the complex and often fragmented knowledge in this rapidly evolving field by establishing chemical composition, processing, microstructure and mechanical properties relationships. For this purpose, a structured search was conducted using Web of Science database, relying on carefully selected keywords and topics for a complete overview to identify relevant studies.

To attain the main goal, the following partial objectives are addressed: Systematically analyze the interplay between compositional modifications and LPBF processability. This involves a critical examination of how specific elemental additions alter the alloys’ microstructure and properties, thereby influencing the viable processing window, defect susceptibility, and the need for parameter re-optimization. Synthesize and map the mechanical properties of LPBF MHEAs, both as-built and after post-processing. Identify current challenges and knowledge gaps, pointing towards future research directions.

To achieve the objectives the paper is organized in 7 sections. The Introduction contextualizes the fundamental concepts of HEAs, including their core effects, and addresses different HEA families, namely MHEAs. The second section starts with an overview of the additive manufacturing of HEAs, followed by a more detailed analysis of the LPBF technology, from feedstock to post-processing. The third section focus on the causes and effects of defects from LPBF manufacturing and resultant microstructures. The modification strategies, process parameters, and resulting phase composition are addressed in section four. Fifth section explores the mechanical properties of the as-built and post-processed MHEAs. Finally, the primary challenges and limitations hindering the industrial adoption of LPBF-processed MHEAs are outlined in section six, and a forward-looking agenda to address these gaps and accelerate the transition from laboratory-scale to applicable engineering components is proposed. To conclude, a summary of the work is presented.

sections.heading: Additive manufacturing of high entropy alloys
paragraphs: In recent years, AM has undergone significant maturation, driven by remarkable advancements in techniques and materials. As a result, AM has emerged as a prominent focus of research and has garnered considerable attention from manufacturing industries worldwide. The transition of 3D printing to factory floors is no longer a concept but a rapidly unfolding reality. Lux Research, a technology-enabled research and innovation advisory firm based in Boston, Massachusetts, USA, recently published a report titled “Will 3D Printing Replace Conventional Manufacturing?”. This report projects that the Additive Manufacturing market will grow to 51 billion USD within the next decade [ 46 ].

AM processes provide substantial benefits across various industries, contributing positively to the society, economy, and environment by enhancing production sustainability and reducing waste. AM has the capability of producing near-net-shape components with high geometrical and dimensional accuracy with the ability to combine several machining steps into a single production step, which dramatically reduces the fabrication time and lowers costs [ 47 ,  48 ]. AM encompasses a wide array of technologies, broadly classified based on the form of feedstock used (powder, wire, or sheet) and the energy source applied (laser, electron beam, or binder). Among the established AM processes, several have been explored for the fabrication of HEAs, including Powder Bed Fusion (PBF) and Directed Energy Deposition (DED). Each of these methods offers distinct advantages and limitations concerning the processing of complex, multi-principal element alloys like HEAs [ 49 ]. Employing Web of Science’s database, the number of articles per year focusing on HEAs and AM manufactured HEAs is shown in Fig.  3 . During the last decade, work on HEAs has accelerated indicating a growing interest in this field of research. On the other hand, research on AM manufactured HEAs remains in its infancy, with a comparatively limited number of articles, though the number is increasing. Fig. 3 Retrieved articles on HEAs published between January 2015 to December 2025

Among AM techniques, LPBF has emerged as particularly promising for fabricating HEAs, due to its high precision, microstructural control, and ability to produce fully dense parts with complex geometries. LPBF operates by selectively melting thin layers of metallic powder using a high-power laser, offering a tightly controlled thermal environment. This is especially advantageous for HEAs, where microstructural uniformity, elemental homogeneity, and phase stability are critical to achieving the desired mechanical and functional properties. Moreover, the rapid solidification rates inherent to LPBF often lead to unique microstructures, such as refined grains, metastable phases, or suppressed segregation, that are difficult to achieve through conventional processing routes [ 50 ,  51 – 52 ].

sections.heading: Laser powder bed fusion
paragraphs: The application of LPBF to the manufacturing of HEAs represents a critical frontier in the development of advanced structural materials. While previous sections have established the compositional and structural characteristics of HEAs, and the overarching advantages of additive manufacturing, it is within the LPBF domain that the interplay between process parameters, material behavior, and microstructural evolution becomes particularly intricate.

HEAs present both a challenge and an opportunity in the context of LPBF. Their compositional complexity, although the source of many of their advantageous properties, also introduces sensitivity to rapid solidification dynamics, local thermal histories, and elemental vaporization during processing. Achieving homogenous microstructures, phase stability, and defect minimization requires a detailed understanding and rigorous control of LPBF process parameters. Unlike conventional alloys, whose behavior under LPBF has been extensively characterized, HEAs often defy established empirical guidelines due to their non-traditional phase formation tendencies and thermophysical properties. Therefore, the development of predictive strategies is necessary, such as computer assisted phase modeling and tailored design of experiment (DoE) methodologies, to guide composition and parameter selection, optimize build quality, and understand defect formation mechanisms [ 52 ,  53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ].

The challenges inherent in processing HEAs via LPBF are amplified when considering MHEAs. The intentional addition or substitution of elements, even in minor quantities, can significantly alter the alloy's behavior during manufacturing. For instance, elements with high vapor pressures, such as aluminum and manganese, are prone to selective vaporization under the intense energy of the laser, leading to compositional deviations and keyhole porosity. Conversely, the introduction of elements like boron or carbon to form refractory precipitates, can complicate processing by raising the melting temperature locally or leading to unmelted particles, which can act as defect initiation sites. These compositional modifications also directly influence the solidification pathway under rapid cooling, potentially leading to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases or increasing susceptibility to hot cracking. Therefore, the successful LPBF manufacturing of MHEAs requires not only optimizing parameters for the base alloy, but also accounting for the intricate effects of each alloying addition on laser absorption, melt pool dynamics, and phase stability.

sections.heading: Phase prediction
paragraphs: Phase prediction is a fundamental step in the design and development of High Entropy Alloys, particularly when they are processed via Laser Powder Bed Fusion, where rapid solidification and non-equilibrium conditions can lead to complex phase formation. At its core, phase prediction aims to determine which crystallographic phases are thermodynamically stable or metastable at given temperatures and compositions. This insight is essential for ensuring the desired balance between strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and other target properties, all of which are strongly phase dependent.

One of the most robust and widely adopted tools for phase prediction is the calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD). It is a computational approach that combines experimental data, first-principles calculations, and thermodynamic models to construct phase diagrams and predict phase equilibrium across multicomponent systems. By minimizing the Gibbs free energy of a system, the models allow for the prediction of stable phases, phase fractions, transformation temperatures, and even non-equilibrium solidification pathways under conditions relevant to LPBF [ 57 ,  58 ].

In the context of HEAs, CALPHAD is particularly valuable since traditional phase diagram data is scarce or nonexistent for such complex multi-element alloy systems, making empirical design approaches unfeasible. This can be circumvented by utilizing assessed binary and ternary subsystems to extrapolate behavior to higher-order systems, enabling to screen compositions computationally before experimental validation, and significantly accelerating alloy discovery and optimization. The ability to predict phase stability is critical because the mechanical and functional performance of a HEA is intimately linked to its microstructure and phase constitution. For example, single-phase solid solutions, often FCC, BCC, or a combination of both, are desired for their mechanical stability and ductility. In contrast, the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds or excessive phase segregation can severely degrade performance, particularly in load-bearing or high-temperature applications [ 59 ].

Recently, artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as powerful tools to accelerate the design of MHEAs, overcoming the computational limits of traditional CALPHAD methodologies. Specifically, ML models have been successfully deployed to design high-performance multi-principal-element superalloys [ 60 ,  61 ]. Through the integration of supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, it is possible to establish quantitative correlations between the material composition and processing parameters, and the resulting microstructural characteristics. For instance, unsupervised learning techniques, such as K-Means clustering, enable the analysis of first-principles calculations to predict the site occupancy patterns of transition-metal dopants within the L1 2  strengthening phase [ 62 ]. These computational design strategies facilitate rapid exploration of composition spaces with substantially reduced experimental effort, thereby accelerating the optimization of MHEAs suitable for LPBF manufacturing.

A critical limitation in deploying ML for materials design concerns model interpretability and the restricted extrapolative capacity of trained algorithms. To address these constraints, researchers have adopted interpretability frameworks, such as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method, which decompose model predictions into quantifiable contributions from individual input features, thereby elucidating the relationships between material and predicted properties [ 60 ,  61 ]. By identifying optimal ranges for empirical parameters including valence electron concentration, mixing enthalpy, and melting temperature, these rules establish transferable design principles that may be applied without access to the original trained model [ 60 ].

Under LPBF’s rapid cooling and steep thermal gradients, non‑equilibrium phases such as Laves, ordered B2, and quasicrystals can form, typically in segregated cell or interdendritic regions. Laves phases, which often arise from Nb/Mo/Ti‑enriched residual liquid, are hard and brittle. When they appear as continuous films or coarse particles, they can promote crack initiation, and reduce ductility and fatigue resistance [ 63 ]. B2 intermetallics (e.g., NiAl‑type) can develop in Al‑containing systems through short‑range ordering; fine discontinuous B2 precipitates can raise yield strength, but continuous networks diminish work‑hardening and increase cracking susceptibility [ 59 ]. Quasicrystalline dispersoids may form in Al–transition‑metal chemistries under high undercooling; nanoscale particles can enhance hardness, wear, and oxidation resistance, whereas excessive or continuous fractions can cause embrittlement [ 64 ].

Furthermore, the computer models can be integrated with solidification simulations to predict phase evolution during LPBF, including undercooling effects, solidification velocity, and the potential for non-equilibrium phase retention. This capability is instrumental in guiding process parameter optimization, powder chemical composition adjustments, and post-treatment strategies to tailor final microstructures.

The role of phase prediction becomes even more critical, and simultaneously more complex, when applied to Modified High Entropy Alloys. The intentional introduction of minor alloying elements or the adjustment of principal element ratios requires thermodynamic databases to be robust. The predictive models must not only determine the stability of primary solid solution phases, but also accurately forecast the formation and volume fraction of specific secondary phases, such as carbides, borides, or intermetallics, which are often the reason for the modification. The sensitivity of phase stability to minute compositional changes in MHEAs means that even small inaccuracies in the database can lead to significant deviations between predicted and actual phase(s), amplifying the need for experimental validation. This heightened complexity makes phase prediction an indispensable yet challenging tool for designing MHEAs for LPBF, where non-equilibrium effects can further steer the selection of phases influenced by targeted elemental additions.

Although phase prediction in MHEAs is in its first stages, it will serve as a foundational pillar in the design and additive manufacturing of these alloys. It will provide a predictive framework that links composition to microstructure and, ultimately, to performance. Its integration into the LPBF workflow enables a more rational and efficient development of HEAs with controlled phase stability, reduced defects, and enhanced properties.

sections.heading: Feedstock
paragraphs: There are three main methods to produce LPBF powder feedstock: water, gas and plasma atomization (Fig.  4 ). Each method produces powders with different geometry and, in turn, different characteristics. Water atomization, the cheapest of the three methods, produces larger non-spherical particles compared to other methods. These particles are usually angular and jagged, making them less suitable for LPBF. Nevertheless, water-atomized powders are still used in many cases due to the significantly lower production costs [ 65 ]. Gas atomization is by far the most common method for producing powders for LPBF, as it generates spherical particles with minimal satellites. These powders exhibit high quality for LPBF processing and present a favorable balance between cost and quality [ 65 ]. Powders produced by plasma atomization present the most spherical particles and the least satellites of the three methods. These powders present the best quality for LPBF; however, the high cost associated with this technology makes it economically unviable in most cases [ 65 ]. Fig. 4 Different types of powder geometry and their satellites

Among powder production methods, advanced techniques such as the Plasma Rotating Electrode Process (PREP) and Ultrasonic Atomization (UA) are increasingly employed for LPBF feedstock preparation. The PREP method utilizes centrifugal atomization of a consumable electrode melted by a transferred plasma arc, operating in a crucible-free configuration that prevents ceramic inclusion formation from refractory container interactions [ 66 ]. This is particularly advantageous for highly reactive or high-melting-point refractory alloy systems where compositional fidelity is critical, this method produces highly spherical powders with exceptional purity and a near absence of satellites, which enhances powder flowability and packing density in the powder bed [ 67 ]. UA is another powder production method that utilizes high-frequency vibrations, typically generated by piezoelectric transducers, to atomize molten metal, offering tight control over particle size distribution. Both PREP and UA represent new alternative pathways for synthesizing high quality MHEA powders where strict defect mitigation is required [ 68 ]. For pre-alloyed powders of structurally complex materials, like MHEAs, the highly controlled thermal gradients and cooling rates intrinsic to UA can help suppress severe microsegregation within the individual powder particles prior to the LPBF process [ 69 ]. Although the overall throughput of UA is currently more limited compared to industrial-scale gas atomization, its ability to produce highly homogenous and high-purity powders makes it an invaluable technique for niche applications.

The selection and preparation of feedstock powders are critical factors influencing the quality and properties of HEAs produced via LPBF. Two primary approaches can be employed: (1) pre-alloyed powders; or (2) blending elemental powders and alloying in situ. Each method presents distinct advantages and challenges that must be carefully considered [ 70 ,  71 ]. Pre-alloyed powders are typically produced from ingots with the final intended chemical composition to be fabricated via LPBF, which are then atomized. In most cases gas-atomization is used due to the relation between cost and final particle geometry achieved, resulting in a homogenous powder where each individual spherical particle has the intended composition. This uniformity ensures consistent melting behavior and reduces the risk of elemental segregation during the LPBF process. However, producing pre-alloyed HEA powders is cost intensive, due to the complexity of alloying several principal elements due to the multiple remelting times to ensure compositional homogeneity. Additionally, the availability of pre-alloyed powders for novel or less-studied HEA compositions is limited.

Alternatively, blending elemental powders offers greater flexibility in exploring new HEA compositions and can be more economical and time effective. This approach allows for the rapid development and customization of alloy systems. However, challenges include achieving homogeneous mixing and mitigating differences in melting points, densities, and laser absorptivity among the constituent elements. These disparities can lead to incomplete melting, elemental segregation, and lack of homogeneity, affecting phase composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties of the final part. Careful control of process parameters and potential post-processing treatments are often required to address these issues. Other important factors are particle size, geometry and satellites, which critically influence the quality of parts produced via LPBF. Optimal powders for LPBF typically exhibit a particle size distribution ranging from 20 to 45 µm [ 65 ], even though this is the typical range, particle size can be larger (e.g. 55 µm) or smaller (e.g. 15 µm), this range serves as a guide and not a rule. Spherical particles with minimum satellites are particularly desirable, as their geometry promotes superior flowability and packing density, leading to uniform layer deposition and consistent part quality [ 72 ]. Satellites are small and mostly spherical defects aggregated on to a powder particle as shown in Fig.  4 .

sections.heading: Processing
paragraphs: The successful fabrication of HEAs via LPBF requires an understanding of the complex synergistic relationship between alloy composition and process parameters. The inherent compositional complexity of MHEAs means that even minor elemental modifications to base systems can drastically alter the material's thermophysical properties, shifting the viable processing window and dictating the final microstructure and defect susceptibility. Simultaneously, the extreme thermal dynamics of the LPBF process, characterized by superheated melt pools and cooling rates in the ranges of 10 3  K/s to 10 8  K/s [ 73 ], can trigger element-specific behaviors like selective vaporization and micro-segregation, further complicating the translation from powder chemistry to final part composition. However, this sensitivity also presents an opportunity: by systematically tuning process parameters such as laser power, scan speed, and scan strategy, it is possible to exert considerable control over the solidification environment, enabling a degree of in-situ microstructural engineering that is unique to additive manufacturing.

The LPBF process is influenced by the multiple parameters presented in Fig.  5 , grouped into five general areas: laser-related parameters, hatch strategy, powder characteristics, operational temperature, and material. Because the hatch strategy directly dictates the thermal history and defect susceptibility of the build, it is crucial to clearly define its primary components. Hatch speed refers to the scanning velocity of the laser beam as it scans the hatch tracks. Hatch spacing is the lateral distance between adjacent hatch tracks. Hatch thickness denotes the effective depth and width of the individual melt track, which is governed by the selected energy parameters and laser beam diameter. Finally, the hatch pattern describes the geometric strategy of the laser path, such as zig-zag, stripe, or chessboard patterns, which heavily influences local thermal gradients and residual stress accumulation. Fig. 5 General LPBF parameters

The concept of a “process window”, the specific range of LPBF parameters that yields a dense, defect-free part, is not static but is instead a direct function of an alloy's thermophysical properties, including its melting range, thermal conductivity, laser absorptivity, and melt viscosity. When the base composition of an HEA is modified, these properties are altered, which in turn necessitates a re-optimization of the process parameters [ 74 ]. Adding refractory elements like W, Mo, or Nb to a more ductile base system, for example, dramatically increases the melting temperature and can create a wide solidification range, requiring a significant increase in the Volumetric Energy Density (VED) to achieve complete melting and prevent lack-of-fusion porosity [ 75 ]. This is typically accomplished by increasing laser power and/or decreasing scan speed. However, these refractory elements often increase the alloy's susceptibility to thermal cracking due to high thermal stresses and the formation of brittle phases, severely narrowing the viable processing window [ 76 ]. On the other hand, some elemental additions can improve processability. The addition of Ti to a refractory-based system has been shown to enhance mechanical properties, reducing density and making the alloy less susceptible to thermal cracking. However, since Ti is prone to oxidation, the conditions in the build chamber need to be highly controlled [ 77 ,  78 ]. Additions of Al are more complex, while Al can promote the formation of BCC and B2 phases when added to FCC base systems, it also increases melt pool viscosity and is prone to vaporization, requiring a narrower and often lower-energy processing window to avoid keyhole porosity and compositional shifts [ 43 ,  79 ]. Even minor additions of other elements can have profound effects, boron, for instance, is known to segregate to grain boundaries, acting as a strong grain refiner, and disrupting the columnar morphology typical of LPBF, which alters the material's response to thermal stresses and can shift the optimal parameter set [ 80 ]. The vast compositional variety of MHEAs means that predicting the printability of a novel alloy is a significant challenge. This has spurred the development of integrated approaches using CALPHAD thermodynamic calculations and machine learning to create “printability maps”, though this remains a rather unexplored field of research.

The extreme temperatures within the LPBF melt pool can exceed the boiling points of some constituent elements. Selective vaporization is a major concern for alloys containing elements such as Mn, Al and Cr. These elements have a high vapor pressure and will preferentially evaporate from the superheated melt pool, leading to a depletion in the final solidified part [ 81 ]. This effect is cumulative and spatially dependent, becoming more pronounced in regions that experience multiple remelting cycles from overlapping scan tracks and subsequent layers, resulting in chemical inhomogeneity throughout the component. Furthermore, the rapid solidification creates a non-equilibrium environment where elemental diffusion is severely limited [ 82 ]. While this can be beneficial for suppressing the formation of undesired phases, it often leads to micro-segregation. The micro-segregation can be mitigated by parameter manipulation during the LPBF process, for example, an interlayer remelting scan; or after the manufacturing process by post-processing.

sections.heading: Post-processing
paragraphs: Post-processing is an indispensable stage in the LPBF manufacturing chain for High Entropy Alloys, required to transform the as-built "near-net-shape" components into functional engineering parts. Despite the high geometric complexity achievable by LPBF, the process introduces inherent characteristics, such as surface roughness, residual stresses, and the necessity of support structures, that must be addressed to meet stringent dimensional and mechanical standards. Consequently, a sequence of subtractive and finishing operations is typically employed to ensure the final component meets design specifications.

The primary post-processing step involves the separation of the part from the build plate and the removal of support structures. This is most commonly achieved via Wire Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM), which utilizes a charged wire to cut through the metal with high precision [ 83 ]. EDM is preferred over mechanical sawing, due to its ability to minimize material loss and avoid exerting excessive physical force on the part, which is critical for preserving the integrity of delicate features or thin-walled sections [ 84 ].

Following removal, surface quality must be addressed. As-built LPBF parts frequently exhibit high surface roughness caused by the “stair-stepping” effect of layer-by-layer deposition and partially sintered powder particles adhered to the surface. To mitigate this, mechanical surface finishing techniques such as sandblasting and vibratory tumbling are routinely applied to remove loosely attached powder and smooth surface irregularities. For applications requiring superior surface finishes, such as in biomedical or fluid-dynamic components, more advanced methods like electropolishing or abrasive flow machining are employed to reduce roughness at a microscopic level, thereby enhancing fatigue life by minimizing surface crack initiation sites [ 85 ,  86 ].

Dimensional accuracy is another critical factor, as thermal distortions during the build process can lead to deviations from tolerances. To correct these geometric discrepancies, traditional subtractive manufacturing methods, including computer numerical control (CNC) machining and grinding, are integrated into the workflow [ 87 ]. These techniques ensure that critical mating surfaces and tight-tolerance features achieve the necessary precision that LPBF alone cannot guarantee.

Furthermore, mechanical surface treatments are often utilized to enhance surface integrity. Peening techniques, such as shot peening or laser shock peening, are applied to introduce compressive residual stresses into the surface layer of the component [ 88 ]. This modification significantly improves resistance to fatigue and stress corrosion cracking, which is particularly beneficial for MHEAs designed for high-load cyclic applications.

While mechanical and geometric corrections are vital, the microstructural integrity of the alloy remains the defining factor for performance. The rapid solidification inherent to LPBF generates significant internal residual stresses and non-equilibrium microstructures that can compromise ductility and structural stability. To alleviate these stresses and tailor the phase composition of MHEAs, post-processing heat treatment is mandatory. The specific regimes and effects of these thermal cycles, which are the most dominant form of post-processing for property optimization, are discussed in the following section.

sections.heading: Heat treatment
paragraphs: Due to the unique microstructural features, the as-built LPBF microstructure is typically characterized by fine columnar grains, high dislocation densities, pronounced micro and macro segregation, and by the presence of residual stresses and porosity. These characteristics, while sometimes beneficial for certain mechanical properties, can also lead to undesirable brittleness, anisotropy, and reduced ductility, thereby limiting the applicability of as-built components for demanding engineering applications [ 11 ]. To unlock these engineering applications, several types of heat treatments are employed for LPBF-fabricated HEAs, each tailored to address specific microstructural and property requirements. Depending on the heat treatment temperature, it can be used to tailor the phase composition, precipitates’ distribution, and grain size, thereby optimizing the strength/ductility trade-off. Depending on the engineering application of the alloy, the ideal temperature for specific phase formation can be calculated by resorting to a computer assisted phase prediction model.

There are three main types of heat treatment employed in LPBF manufactured HEAs: Annealing involves heating the material above its recrystallization temperature, usually in an inert atmosphere, maintaining a specific temperature for a suitable period, and then allowing it to cool in a controlled way, typically inside the furnace. During annealing, atoms in the crystal lattice can migrate, moving more freely, reducing the number of dislocations, relieving internal stresses and homogenizing, which typically results in a softer and more ductile material. Annealing can also promote the formation of specific phases or precipitates to improve properties. When the temperature is guided by the phase diagram of the specific HEA, it is possible to target these specific phases/intermetalics. In MHEAs, intermetallics are typically face-centered cubic L 1 2  phase or the body-centered cubic B2 phase. The size, morphology, and distribution of these precipitates are strictly controlled by the annealing temperature and duration [ 89 ,  90 – 91 ]. Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) is a process that combines high temperature and isostatic gas pressure, to densify materials and eliminate cracks and porosity. The main objective of HIP is to improve mechanical properties such as mechanical strength, fracture toughness, and fatigue resistance, by achieving near-theoretical density and closing internal defects. HIP subjects the component to high temperatures, and high isostatic gas pressure in the range of 100 to 200 MPa, simultaneously [ 92 ]. This combination activates creep and diffusion mechanisms that effectively collapse internal voids, including lack-of-fusion defects and gas porosity, which are difficult to eliminate via conventional annealing. The densification achieved by HIP significantly enhances fatigue life by removing internal crack initiation sites. Furthermore, the thermal exposure during HIP acts as a high-temperature homogenization treatment, promoting the dissolution of segregated elements and brittle interdendritic phases. Recent studies on refractory HEAs, such as WTaMoNbV, have demonstrated that HIP not only increases density but also improves ductility by healing micro-cracks and reducing sub-grain boundary density [ 93 ]. This densification effect as also been shown to result in a significant improvement of the mechanical properties, in a study by Liu et al. [ 94 ] the yield strength increased from 600 to 1100 MPa, an improvement of 83%.

paragraphs: Defects are inherent to LPBF processing, which also results in distinctive microstructures.

sections.heading: Defects
paragraphs: Defects in the LPBF process can arise from various sources, including powder characteristics, material properties, process parameters, and machine configurations. Careful optimization of these factors is essential to minimize defects and ensure high-quality parts. Understanding the causes of defects is crucial to improving the reliability of the process, achieving the desired mechanical and functional properties, and ensuring consistent part quality in targeted applications [ 52 ,  53 ]. Defects can have one or multiple causes, which makes correcting the parameters responsible for the defect a complex operation. Furthermore, they can interact with each other in unexpected ways, adding an additional layer of complexity to defect mitigation [ 52 ,  53 ]. Table  1  lists the main defects that can occur in LPBF manufacturing, together with their possible cause(s) and effect(s). The quality and performance of LPBF-fabricated HEAs are critically governed by the presence of process-induced defects, which are categorized into porosity, cracking, metallurgical, and geometric defects. Porosity-related defects are primarily of three types, each linked to specific melt pool phenomena. Lack of Fusion (LOF) porosity presents as sharp, irregular voids located between scan tracks or layers, resulting from insufficient VED (e.g. low laser power or high scan speed) that prevents complete melting and fusion. These defects act as severe stress concentrators, providing clear initiation sites for fatigue cracks and significantly reducing mechanical properties. In contrast, keyhole porosity arises from excessive energy density, which causes metal vaporization and the formation of an unstable, deep vapor cavity. The collapse of this keyhole, traps gas, leading to the formation of spherical pores that, while less damaging than LOF porosity, still deteriorates mechanical properties and can nucleate fatigue cracks. A third type, entrapped gas porosity, consists of small, spherical voids originating from gas trapped within the initial powder feedstock or absorbed from the build chamber environment, which further contributes to a reduction in overall density and ductility.

Cracking is among the most detrimental defects, with two main forms prevalent in LPBF of HEAs. Hot cracking, or solidification cracking, manifests as intergranular cracks that form in the semi-solid zone during the final stages of solidification. It is driven by thermal cycles acting on a microstructure weakened by low-melting-point liquid films that can form at grain boundaries due to elemental segregation, a known risk in multi-element HEAs with wide solidification ranges. Conversely, cold cracking occurs in the cooling stage, driven by the accumulation of high tensile residual stresses, due to rapid heating and cooling cycles of the LPBF process. If these stresses exceed the material's yield strength, particularly in brittle or strain-sensitive microstructures, cracks can initiate and propagate, severely compromising the structural integrity of the part. These cracks usually propagate in the build direction, for each deposited layer the cracks tend to grow as they experience additional thermal cycles.

Beyond porosity and cracking, several metallurgical and geometric defects can degrade component quality. Non-metallic inclusions, such as oxides, can be introduced from contaminated or improperly recycled powder or through reactions with residual oxygen in the build chamber, acting as internal stress concentrators that are highly detrimental to fatigue life. Similarly, spatter, molten droplets ejected from the melt pool, can contaminate the surrounding powder bed and become partially melted inclusions in subsequent layers. At a larger scale, unstable melt pools can lead to balling, where the molten metal forms discontinuous beads instead of a continuous track, resulting in high surface roughness and large internal voids. This excessive surface roughness itself serves as a stress concentrator and a prime location for fatigue crack initiation. The extreme cooling rates of LPBF can also induce micro-segregation of alloying elements to dendritic or cellular boundaries, creating chemical and mechanical heterogeneities and potentially promoting the formation of brittle, non-equilibrium phases. Finally, the accumulation of residual stress can cause macroscopic distortion, warping, and even delamination (separation of layers), compromising the dimensional accuracy and structural integrity of the final component. Therefore, achieving defect-free HEA parts requires an integrated approach that simultaneously controls process parameters to stabilize the melt pool, manages thermal gradients to minimize residual stress, and ensures high-purity feedstock and chamber environment to prevent contamination.

In MHEAs, compositional adjustments can intensify or introduce defect mechanisms during LPBF, narrowing the processing window and complicating mitigation strategies. Additions that increase volatility elevate the risk of selective vaporization, keyhole instability, and composition drift, while ordering, or segregation promoting elements foster brittle networks or interdendritic films that act as crack initiation sites [ 122 ]. For example, Al bearing AlxCoCrFeNi systems frequently develop coexisting BCC/B2 phases in the as built state. Ordered B2 networks and elevated thermal stresses have been linked to hot cracking unless high preheating, adapted scan strategies, and post build heat treatments are employed [ 123 ]. Furthermore, compositional tuning can shift the solidification path from one phase toward another, for example, from primarily FCC to BCC/B2, which strengthens the alloy but also increases lack of fusion sensitivity and crack susceptibility if energy density and hatch overlap are not jointly optimized. These cases illustrate that alloy modifications intended to enhance strength or high temperature stability can increase LPBF defect formation window, making defect control inseparable from composition specific process mapping and thermal management.

Efforts to mitigate the defects have included both pre- and post-processing strategies. Processing parameters optimization, implementing a Design of Experiment, is the best tool to significantly reduce not only lack of fusion and keyhole pores, but many other defects as well. As such, defect control remains a critical area of focus in the development of HEAs via LPBF, with future work likely to integrate real-time monitoring, advanced powder preparation techniques, and machine learning-based process optimization.

sections.heading: Advances in process monitoring and control
paragraphs: Recent published studies have significantly advanced the understanding of melt pool dynamics and defect prediction in LPBF. High-fidelity multi-physics simulations have enabled precise modeling of how variations in temperature gradients and recoil pressure influence melt pool stability, capturing complex phenomena like melting, solidification, and fluid flow behavior [ 124 ]. Furthermore, researchers are increasingly employing deep learning algorithms to achieve super-resolution reconstruction of melt pool monitoring images, allowing for the extraction of boundary information [ 125 ]. These physics-based insights are now being actively coupled with ML techniques to predict lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity with remarkable accuracy. By capturing 3D point clouds in real time via binocular vision, deep learning models can perform high-precision defect segmentation directly during the printing process [ 126 ]. Additionally, integrating deep learning neural networks with traditional ML algorithms allows for the extraction of multidimensional feature information from surface morphologies, significantly improving the prediction accuracy of relative density and part densification [ 127 ].

The unique and rapid thermal cycles of the LPBF process dictate the microstructural evolution and structural integrity of the manufactured components. To capture these complex phenomena, recent research has placed a strong emphasis on continuous thermal history monitoring and modeling. Thermo-mechanical finite element simulations are now routinely utilized to analyze the influence of process parameters, such as laser speed and hatch spacing, on localized cooling rates and thermal gradients [ 128 ]. This thermal data is crucial for understanding the accumulation of residual stresses, which can be computationally predicted by integrating the component's layer-by-layer temperature history into improved inherent strain methodologies [ 129 ]. Monitoring the thermal history allows for a deeper comprehension of how transient thermal states trigger deformation, phase transformations, and thermal stress formation in the manufactured parts [ 130 ]. By predicting the residual stress states, it is possible to map specific thermal signatures directly to the final mechanical properties, helping to mitigate phenomena such as accelerated fatigue crack growth caused by anisotropic tensile stresses in near-surface regions [ 131 ].

Building upon predictive models and real-time monitoring, intelligent process control has emerged as a critical frontier for ensuring the structural reliability of LPBF-manufactured alloys. A key component of this transition involves the development of efficient closed-loop control strategies that utilize multi-sensor in situ detection, combining optical and thermal methods to adjust laser parameters on the fly to prevent defect formation [ 132 ]. Intelligent systems can automatically compensate for process drift by optimizing laser scanning strategies and orientations, actively reducing thermal stress accumulation through targeted modifications to scan vector lengths and interlayer rotation angles [ 133 ]. Furthermore, advanced thermal modeling techniques, such as experiment-based superposition models utilizing discrete Green's functions, are being deployed to predict temperature distributions and enable feedforward control corrections during multi-track scanning [ 134 ]. This shift from passive monitoring to active, algorithm-driven process control is essential for managing the complex, multi-scale evolution of residual stresses and thermal gradients during manufacturing [ 135 ]. Ultimately, these intelligent frameworks facilitate the reliable, defect-free scaling of advanced additive manufacturing technologies for demanding industrial applications.

sections.heading: Compositional design and microstructure
paragraphs: The microstructural characteristics of HEAs manufactured by LPBF are fundamentally governed by the alloy’s composition, but primarily, the extreme thermal conditions inherent to the process, resulting in unique microstructures that significantly differ from those obtained through conventional manufacturing routes [ 136 ]. The rapid heating and cooling cycles experienced during processing, with cooling and heating rates ranging from 103 to 10⁸ K/s, create non-equilibrium solidification conditions that inhibit grain growth and promote the formation of fine microstructures with improved mechanical properties [ 137 ,  138 ].

Different design strategies have resulted in seven unique classes of LPBF-fabricated HEAs, each displaying different properties as a result of distinct microstructures [ 139 ]. As an example, Fig.  6  shows microscopy images of a CrMnFeCoNi Cantor HEA manufactured by LPBF. The AlCo 0.4 CrFeNi 2.7  alloy develops a dual-phase (FCC + BCC) microstructure, where the BCC phase grows around the FCC lamellae. The EDS maps (Fig.  7 c) indicate that the FCC lamellae are rich in Fe, Co and Cr elements, while the BCC lamellae are rich in Ni and Al elements [ 140 ]. Phase variety in HEAs significantly influences the mechanical properties of the final components, with FCC-based alloys typically exhibiting excellent ductility and fracture toughness, but relatively lower mechanical strength, with yield strengths around 200–900 MPa and elongations of 20–50% [ 13 ]. In contrast, BCC and B2 phases provide significantly higher strength, with yield strengths ranging from 800 to 1400 MPa, but at the expense of ductility, which typically ranges from 0 to 15% [ 33 ]. The formation of dual-phase microstructures can provide an optimal balance between strength and ductility by utilizing the high strength of BCC phases and the good ductility of FCC phases [ 40 ].

In MHEAs, deliberate compositional deviations from a base HEA directly reshape solidification pathways and post-solidification kinetics in LPBF, yielding tailored microstructures that translate into application-specific mechanical and functional responses. Adjusting principal-element ratios modulates phase stability and fractions, shifting FCC/BCC/B2/HCP balances. Minor alloying additions at low atomic percent further engineer the microstructure: C, B, N interstitials precipitate fine carbides/borides/nitrides for dispersion strengthening and creep/wear resistance. Al or Si can stabilize ordered B2 or form protective scales that improve oxidation resistance, Mo/Cr can adjust segregation and corrosion behavior, and Mn/Ni variations can tune stacking-fault energy to activate TWIP/TRIP for enhanced ductility and strain-hardening [ 141 ,  142 ]. Under LPBF’s rapid cooling, these modifications frequently refine cells/grains, intensify elemental partitioning, and stabilize metastable, or nanoscale ordered domains, enabling high yield strength with retained ductility in duplex FCC + B2 systems, very high hardness and wear resistance in BCC/B2-dominated states, or superior fracture toughness and fatigue resistance in FCC-rich matrices with deformation twinning. Consequently, composition design in MHEAs becomes a primary lever to co-optimize microstructure and properties for service (strength–ductility balance, creep and wear resistance, corrosion/oxidation performance, and, where relevant, magnetic/electrical behavior), with post-build heat treatments used to dissolve deleterious films and stabilize the intended phase topology for reliable performance [ 11 ,  80 ,  143 ].

sections.heading: Cantor system
paragraphs: The main modifications of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) alloy are represented in Table  2 . These modifications can have the objectives of melt pool stabilization in the case of the removal of manganese, phase engineering with the addition of titanium, molybdenum and niobium, and interstitial strengthening with the addition of carbon.

The most studied modification to the Cantor system is the removal of manganese to form the quaternary CoCrFeNi alloy. This strategy primarily addresses the negative effects of manganese volatility. Manganese possesses high vapor pressure that significantly increases with temperature, often leading to vaporization in the melt pool. In the base Cantor alloy, this excessive volatilization can induce keyhole defects, significant fume generation, and compositional shifts, which frequently result in porosity and segregation. By eliminating this volatile species, the quaternary system has a more stable melt pool. The entries 8, 11 and 12 show that the manganese elimination results in a broader processing window, high relative densities (> 99.7%) are achieved at both low power (94 W) and high power (320 W) regimes. The VED varies significantly from 52.7 to 128.2 J/mm 3  without compromising density, indicating that the exclusion of Mn broadens the processing window. The alloy also retains its original single-phase FCC structure, indicating that Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni have high mutual solubility and resist forming intermetallics in the absence of strong precipitate-formers like Ti or Al [ 148 ,  149 – 150 ].

The introduction of elements, such as Ti, Mo and Nb into the CoCrFeNi system marks a transition from a single-phase solid solution to a complex, multi-phase alloy. The mechanism governing this multi-phase transition is driven by the severe lattice distortion and highly negative mixing enthalpy introduced by the oversized Ti, Mo, and Nb solute atoms. To relieve this resulting internal strain, the system exceeds its solid solubility limit and precipitates secondary intermetallic compounds to minimize overall thermodynamic free energy [ 169 ,  170 ]. This strategy aims to overcome the yield strength limitations of the FCC matrix, though it increases processing challenges due to the high melting points and brittle nature of the resulting phases. In entries 6, 7, 10, 15, 16, 18 and 19 these elements were added with mixed results. In studies where only Ti was added (10, 15 and 16) HCP and BCC phases, as well as NiTi, were formed from the original FCC matrix, though these phases only started to appear at high titanium contents, at least higher than ~ 7 at.%, below Ti did not have impact in phase balancing [ 153 ]. The combination of Ti and Mo also seems to have a special dynamic due to the creation of Single Cubic (SC) phase, a phase that is not created by any other modification in this system, which is another good example of how different elements have complex dynamics between each other, and are important to consider while designing MHEAs [ 128 ,  129 – 130 ,  134 ].

Furthermore, carbon microalloying in Cantor-type systems introduces mechanistic shifts in solidification pathways and defect susceptibility. Interstitial carbon atoms pin dislocations and expand the lattice, providing robust solid-solution strengthening. Crucially, under the rapid thermal cycles of LPBF, carbon tends to segregate to grain boundaries, nucleating nanoscale carbides. These fine precipitates act as heterogeneous nucleation sites within the melt pool, disrupting the epitaxial grain growth that usually dominates LPBF processing, and promoting a columnar-to-equiaxed transition, which effectively mitigates the anisotropic mechanical behavior [ 171 ,  172 ].

sections.heading: AlCrFeCoNi system
paragraphs: The equiatomic AlCrFeCoNi alloy serves as a distinct base system compared to the Cantor system. While Cantor is single-phase FCC, the high aluminum content in the base AlCrFeCoNi system drives the formation of a BCC dominated structure, often accompanied by ordered B2 phases. The modifications to this system primarily aim to introduce ductility via FCC stabilization or to enhance specific mechanical properties through precipitation, utilizing strategies like Al-depletion, Mn-addition, and element substitution.

The most critical variable in this alloy system is the aluminum content, being a strong BCC stabilizer [ 173 ]. The mechanism driving this transformation begins with the incorporation of aluminum that destabilizes the close-packed FCC matrix, as its comparatively larger atomic radius induces severe lattice distortion and increases internal strain energy. To relieve this thermodynamic instability, the system minimizes its overall free energy by nucleating the less densely packed BCC phase, transitioning into a dual-phase microstructure [ 174 ,  175 ]. The base system is processed at 350 W and yields BCC + B2 + A2 phase [ 157 ]. In entry 22, a modification is studied, it effectively halves the Al content relative to the other elements. This Al reduction alters the thermodynamic landscape, moving the alloy from the single-phase BCC region into the FCC + BCC dual-phase region, where the FCC phase provides ductility while the retained BCC phase ensures high yield strength. The modification was used with in-situ alloying, with a higher VED compared to the baseline system, it was capable to achieve a high relative density, of 99.92%, indicating a porosity decrease and the viability of in-situ alloying [ 158 ].

In the works corresponding to entries 23 and 24, Mn was added in different amounts, while also reducing the Al content, this modification yielded a dual phase FCC + BCC alloy, impacting significantly process parameters. For this modification a lower VED was employed to process the alloy (59.5 J/mm 3 ), which, compared to the 97.2 J/mm 3  for the baseline, corresponds to a 39% decrease, while maintaining a relative density close to 100% [ 159 ]. Manganese has lower boiling point compared to Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni, a lower VED minimizes Mn vaporization while allowing sufficient time (low hatch speed) to fully melt the feedstock, reducing keyhole instability and deviation from the target composition.

The substitution of Cr for Ti (entry 25) and Ta and B (entry 27), resulted in a single-phase FCC alloy, while utilizing a lower power than the baseline [ 160 ]. In entry 29 the base system was reinforced with Cr 3 C 2 , inducing a complete columnar-to-equiaxed transition, yielding a significantly refined grain microstructure. Elemental partitioning of chromium and carbon to the interdendritic regions and grain boundaries promoted the development of a continuous FCC network along the grain boundaries. In contrast, the grain interiors remained predominantly BCC/B2, punctuated by dispersed Cr 3 C 2  precipitates [ 142 ].

sections.heading: NbMoTaTiZr system
paragraphs: RHEAs are designed for high working temperature applications, primarily utilizing refractory elements (Nb, Mo, Ta, W). Unlike the FCC-based Cantor, these alloys predominantly crystallize in a BCC structure. The modifications highlighted in Table  2  show a distinct trade-off between processability and chemical composition. The resistance to high working temperatures, inherent to refractory elements, makes these alloys more complex to process via LPBF, requiring higher VEDs. Due to the low ductility of these alloys with BCC matrix, cracking associated to thermal cycles is also a major concern.

In entries 30 and 31 the base system was manufactured using in situ alloying and relatively low laser power, 280W and 300W, and high speeds, 1200 mm/s and 1000 mm/s, respectively, leading to low VEDs [ 163 ]. Low VEDs are not suitable for in situ alloying of this alloy system since the relative density is low, 97% and 75%, indicating that the internal porosity is considerably high, especially in entry 31. Comparing these two entries with 32, it is clear the impact that pre-alloying feedstock has in this type of system. Processing the alloy with a lower laser power and higher hatch speed it was possible to achieve a 99.82% relative density, indicating the reduced porosity of the final specimen [ 149 ,  150 ,  165 ].

A common modification to the base system is the substitution of one element, usually zirconium, with tungsten. Due to the difference in melting point of these two elements, this substitution has a significant processing impact, meaning that the energy to melt the feedstock also need to be increased impacting in the VEDs utilized, especially in entries 33 and 34, the highest VEDs in Table  2 , 666.7 J/mm 3 , achieving high relative density [ 166 ]. Microalloying the alloys with carbon has shown promising results, without influencing the processing window. A new alloy exhibiting a BCC matrix with NbC precipitates was studied by J. Xu et al., demonstrating that the precipitates positively affect the mechanical properties of the alloy while achieving almost porosity-free specimens [ 166 ].

In modification 35, zirconium was substituted by nickel, resulting in the suppression of crack formation and defects during LPBF processing, while maintaining the original BCC matrix, as well as not severely impacting the processing window [ 167 ].

In Table  3 , three compositional systems fall onto distinct strength-ductility regimes: ductile FCC Cantor‑type derivatives with moderate strength, AlCrFeCoNi variants that leverage FCC and BCC for balanced properties, and refractory BCC systems that maximize strength, mainly in compression at the expense of tensile ductility. This organization reflects process‑enabled control of phase selection and defect content under rapid solidification, providing a composition–processing–microstructure–property pathway that can be intentionally navigated for specific application performance in LPBF.

Within the Cantor family, the base CoCrFeMnNi remains single‑phase FCC after LPBF and typically exhibits yield strengths on the order o500 to ~ 900 MPa, with tensile elongations frequently spanning from ~ 20 to 50%. Modifications that insert interstitials, such as C, raise strength through stacking fault energy tuning and fine carbide formation, while partially preserving uniform strain, whereas substitutional elements, like Ti, promote secondary phases (e.g., BCC/Laves) that elevate hardness and yield strength at a measurable ductility penalty, mirroring LPBF trends for Cantor derivatives reported broadly in the literature [ 140 ,  141 ]. These observations underscore that light interstitial additions are an efficient route to strengthen FCC matrices without fully sacrificing the formability that makes Cantor-based alloys attractive.

Al‑bearing AlCrFeCoNi systems pivot the matrix toward BCC, yielding dual‑phase FCC + BCC microstructures, typically with retained B2 within the BCC regions and L1 2  precipitates within FCC, which together deliver substantial hardness and compressive strength while enabling tunable toughness via phase fraction control. Entries that deliberately introduce carbide inoculants (e.g., Cr 3 C 2 ) reveal columnar‑to‑equiaxed grain transitions and significant refinement, illustrating how heterogeneous nucleation can break epitaxy, reduce texture, and help distribute strain more uniformly under LPBF thermal gradients. As a result, carefully calibrated Al contents and post‑processing precipitation treatments offer a practical knob to balance strength and ductility in this family, positioning AlCrFeCoNi derivatives as candidates for applications requiring higher static strength than Cantor alloys, and greater toughness than refractory BCC alloys.

Refractory BCC alloys, such as NbMoTaW, attain the highest hardness and compressive strength, often in the ~ 1700 to 2300 MPa range (Table  3 ), yet show limited ductility at room temperature, a consequence of constrained slip that LPBF’s steep thermal gradients can intensify through residual stresses and microcrack sensitivity [ 177 ]. Alloying with Ti, W and C (table entries 41 to 45) can raise yield strength further and, in favorable cases, modestly improve ductility via grain refinement and dislocation storage, although without fully overcoming the intrinsic brittleness of these alloys under tensile loads, which aligns with recent LPBF literature on refractory HEAs, incorporating precipitation‑strengthening and crack‑mitigation strategies [ 166 ,  168 ]. Consequently, refractory MHEAs are best matched to compression‑dominated or elevated‑temperature applications, where the combination of their exceptional mechanical strength with improved ductility can be exploited.

Across families, the composition levers are coherent: Al and Ti additions promote ordering and BCC fractions that drive up hardness and yield strength. Interstitials, such as C, elevate strength with small ductility penalties by modifying stacking fault energy and enabling fine precipitates, while intentional particle additions (e.g. carbides) can refine grains and trigger columnar‑to‑equiaxed transitions that mitigate anisotropy and local strain concentrations.

For design and application, these data support three practical guidelines: (1) choose interstitially strengthened FCC Cantor‑type HEAs when room‑temperature ductility and tolerance to geometric complexity are paramount; (2) select AlCrFeCoNi derivatives tuned to dual-phase FCC + BCC with controlled B2/L1 2  precipitation for balanced strength and ductility; and (3) reserve NbMoTaW‑class refractory alloys for compression‑dominated or high‑temperature applications, while leveraging W/Ti additions, carbide precipitation, and defect control to reduce brittleness. Such guidelines are congruent with contemporary LPBF HEA reviews/literature that advocate composition‑specific processing windows, inoculation or preheating for crack‑prone chemical compositions, and targeted post‑processing treatments.

sections.heading: Post-processed
paragraphs: In most cases, post-processing of LPBF MHEAs is a necessary step, although scarcely explored in the literature. Post-processes applied to MHEAs are presented in Table  4 , together with their effects on mechanical properties. Post-processing primarily involves heat treatments (HT) with controlled temperatures and times and hot isostatic pressing, tuning porosity, phase balance, and precipitate topology to shift strength–ductility trade-offs in ways consistent with established literature on additively manufactured HEAs. In short, HIP tend to improve densification and compositional homogeneity with impact on mechanical properties, while heat treatments like aging in Al-containing systems activates B2/L1 2  strengthening, which evidently raises yield strength with ductility decrease.
