In the Cantor family, HIP is applied to the single‑phase FCC matrix at 1150 °C/150 MPa for 3 h, a regime that predominantly closes lack‑of‑fusion and gas pores, relaxes residual stresses, and smooths microsegregation without driving deleterious phase changes, which in turn typically improves ductility and reduces property scatter, while leaving yield strength largely governed by solid‑solution hardening and grain size [ 144 ]. Complementarily, solution treatments near 1120 °C followed by air or water cooling for Ti‑modified compositions (table entries 5, 6, and 7) serve to dissolve interdendritic Laves‑type phases and reset compositional gradients, which promotes uniform strain, while avoiding significant variations in the mechanical properties.

The AlCrFeCoNi base system displays the strongest post‑processing sensitivity, heat treatment unlocks ordered B2 in BCC regions and L1 2  and L2 1  in any retained FCC, which jointly elevate strength, a trend reflected by the table’s dual‑phase entries (11 and 13) that employ annealing to increase YS and UTS, up to 75% and 50%, respectively; with elongations heavily reducing in the mid‑teens [ 160 ].

In entries 15 and 16, two different heat treatments were carried out to provide an instructive contrast: a higher‑temperature and longer HT (950 °C/6 h) that produces a dual‑phase BCC(37%) + FCC(63%) structure, versus a lower‑temperature and short HT (750 °C/3 h) that shifts ordering to favor BCC phase, with BCC(72%) + FCC(28%) structure [ 162 ]. The former HT favors a higher maximum elongation, while the latter targets a higher yield strength at the expense of ductility, illustrating the classic strength/ductility balance that governs dual‑phase HEAs under LPBF. The consistency of these post-processing results with ordered‑precipitation theory in rapidly solidified AlCrFeCoNi, reinforces the utility of these post-processes for specific alloy applications, in order to achieve the desired mechanical properties balance.
Although the post-processing of MHEAs is usually required, the literature is still scarce on what concerns its influence on the mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Challenges, limitations and future directions
paragraphs: Modified high‑entropy alloys offer exciting opportunities for tailored properties, but maturation is constrained by the interplay of complex chemical compositions with rapid, non‑equilibrium processing. This section briefly outlines the overarching challenges and limitations, shaping current capabilities and pathways toward reliable and scalable implementation. Application of these alloys is further hampered by limited standards for AM-processed HEAs, in particularMHEAs.

Thermodynamic databases and solidification models still struggle to predict phase stability, ordering, and segregation due to LPBF’s steep gradients, underscoring the need for tighter integration of computer assisted phase prediction models, solidification modeling, and in-situ diagnostics. Despite advances in high-throughput and combinatorial methods, the composition–processing–microstructure–property relationships for MHEAs is incomplete, slowing down statistically robust optimization across composition and process parameter.

A major challenge associated to the MHEAs processed by LPBF is to guarantee that the feedstock—pre‑alloyed or blended elemental powders for in‑situ alloying—has the designed chemical composition and presents compositional uniformity, at an appropriate cost. In addition, powder morphology and size distribution can constrain processability.

MHEAs intentionally introduce elemental additions that alter melt‑pool dynamics and solidification pathways, raising risks of selective vaporization of volatile elements, composition drift, and keyhole porosity under high energy densities. Refractory elements and elements with strong segregation capacity (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W or Si in certain systems) can partition to interdendritic regions and boundaries, nucleating brittle films and promoting hot cracking under rapid solidification. In refractory modifications, low‑temperature brittleness and challenging LPBF processability remain critical. Even when densification is adequate, subtle composition shifts at the voxel scale can promote the formation of deleterious phases that reduce ductility and fatigue resistance. Non-equilibrium solidification under LPBF promotes Laves and ordered B2 phases and, for selected compositions metastable or quasicrystalline dispersoids, which can strengthen the alloy when refined and discontinuous, but embrittle particularly when coarsened or continuous. The combined effects of ordering, segregation, and rapid thermal cycling complicate phase control in MHEAs, making FCC + BCC/B2 duplex structures attractive, yet fragile. Foundational uncertainties persist in phase‑formation rules for complex HEAs, requiring careful coupling of computational thermodynamics with experimental data for each modified chemical composition.

The narrow LPBF processing window of MHEAs intensifies sensitivity to lack‑of‑fusion, keyhole porosity, balling, spatter entrapment, and both hot and residual stress cracking, hindering scale‑up and consistent quality. Other challenges include as-built anisotropy, lack of reproducibility, and sensitivity to specific machine conditions. High cooling rates, although beneficial for grain refinement, increase thermal gradients and residual stresses, amplifying cracking susceptibility unless preheating, scan‑strategy adaptation, and/or post‑processing stress relief are applied. Generic heat‑treatment protocols from conventional alloys often fail to translate due to sluggish diffusion, ordering tendencies, and metastable phase retention in LPBF MHEAs.

Corrosion behavior can be highly sensitive to micro‑segregation and surface quality in LPBF builds, with porosity and elemental partitioning serving as crack initiation sites, unless mitigated by parameter optimization and post‑processing. Ensuring long‑term phase stability under cyclic thermal exposure is challenging in MHEAs, necessitating tailored corrosion‑resistant compositions and post-processing heat treatments.

Addressing the above challenges and limitations will expand the design possibilities while tightening processing tolerances and increasing qualification burdens for complex parts. The research directions can include the integration of CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling with machine-learning frameworks for composition and process optimization, the expanded use of high-speed diagnostic techniques to resolve transient melt-pool and solidification phenomena, and the development of standardized processing and qualification routes optimized to LPBF-processed MHEAs. Simultaneously, emerging voxel‑scale strategies for graded microstructure and composition in LPBF promise functionally optimized MHEAs in the near future.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: A comprehensive review from existing literature was compiled and analyzed, aiming at identifying processing windows and tradeoffs, and establishing chemical composition, microstructure and mechanical properties relationships. The literature also indicates a gradual shift from exploring equiatomic alloys toward designing MHEAs with compositions tailored for additive manufacturing. While LPBF offers considerable flexibility for controlling microstructure and properties, it also creates strong interactions between feedstock characteristics, processing parameters, and solidification behavior.

Pre-alloyed powders remain the most reliable option for achieving compositional homogeneity, whereas in-situ alloying offers greater flexibility but requires stricter control of processing conditions. At the same time, compositional changes can narrow the LPBF processing window, as volatile elements increase evaporation losses and refractory additions may promote cracking.

Overall, MHEA deployment is constrained by coupled challenges in feedstock quality, composition control, defect mitigation, and phase stability under LPBF, compounded by cost, sustainability, and qualification hurdles. Addressing all these aspects will require coordinated advances in improved computer-assisted phase prediction models, powder technology, in-situ process monitoring, composition-aware parameter mapping, and high-throughput validation to establish reliable composition–processing–microstructure–property relationships for industrial adoption.
